source.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Arthur Conmy; Lewis Smith; Tom Lieberum; Vikrant Varma; J'anos Kram'ar; Rohin Shah; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAE training architectures and losses, measuring shrinkage and reconstruction fidelity. It refines the training-artifact version of the claim, but does not analyze the structure or predictability of SAE residual error.
record.gate_note: Relevant results measure reconstruction bias and language-model loss after SAE reconstructions are spliced in. The paper does not test linear predictability of the residual, tokenwise error scaling or overlap of error contexts across SAE sizes, random-error comparisons, dark-matter components, or downstream behavior lost by omitting the error. Individual sweep points are shown in figures and tables; the rows below record the reported aggregate findings.
record.test_reason: The paper predates the dark-matter framing but shows that changing SAE architecture and loss (Gated vs L1 baseline) lowers reconstruction error, measured as loss recovered at fixed L0. It also separates shrinkage from other training effects. This bears on V6 (error as a training artifact). It does not analyse the structure of the error, so V1–V5 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Missing points: the authors report Gated SAEs need about half the L0 for the same loss recovered at many sites, and that features are comparably interpretable. Their gain over a shrinkage-only fix is attributed to better encoder and decoder directions.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces a gated encoder and a loss applying the sparsity penalty to the gating path, rather than testing the original study’s dark-matter measurements or residual-error analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Baseline shrinkage worsens as the L1 coefficient increases and L0 decreases. Results also vary by model site and layer; the Gemma-7B layer 27 attention-output evaluation has a noted dataset-related anomaly.
record.problems: The reported shrinkage and fidelity measures do not characterize the residual error’s structure. Several results are presented as plots without numerical values in the text; the Gemma-7B layer 27 attention-output result is affected by a training/evaluation dataset mismatch.
record.rows_left_out: Individual L1-coefficient, L0, layer, and site sweep points in Figures 5–6, 12–14 and Tables 1–8 are not listed separately; the rows record the paper’s aggregate statements where available. The individual plotted and tabulated points are not needed to establish the reported aggregate shrinkage and Pareto-frontier findings.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from the input activation.
Per-token error norm prediction, overlap of failing contexts across SAE sizes, and persistence of error with scale.
Comparison of spliced-reconstruction loss against random errors of equal norm.
Split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts and their response to more dictionary learning.
Behaviour lost in circuits or steering when the error term is dropped.
Dead latents and end-to-end training as explanations. Also untested: what fraction of the error is attributable to training versus representation structure.

missing.what: Inference-time optimisation (gradient pursuit) with fixed decoders. Gated dictionaries are slightly better, but the best baseline dictionary (L0≈99) is comparable to the best gated (L0≈20). The encoder-to-ITO gap is smaller for gated. This bears on how much error comes from the encoder versus the dictionary.
Per-site numeric loss recovered and γ for Gated vs baseline SAEs, showing how much error remains after the architecture change (e.g. Gemma MLP L6 gated 73.7–90.7% vs baseline 42–75%).

record.verdict_notes: This is a pre-dark-matter architecture paper, so its bearing on V6 is indirect: loss recovered is a proxy for error size. It is not one of the original sources. The reader's 'supports' label on R2/R3 overstated things; shrinkage removal matters for V6 only via R4, which shows it is a small contributor.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the SAE error vector is a linear function of the input activation.
Whether per-token error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and error persists with scale.
No comparison of model loss under SAE reconstruction against random errors of the same size.
No decomposition of error into learned-feature and nonlinear components, or test of whether those components resist further dictionary learning.
No measurement of behavior lost from SAE-feature-based circuits or steering when the error term is omitted.

The study measures shrinkage and reconstruction fidelity under changed SAE training methods, but does not quantify what fraction of dark matter is due to training, analyze residual structure directly, or test dead latents and end-to-end training as explanations.

rows.subject: GELU-1L
rows.operation_detail: Compared gated SAEs with baseline SAEs trained using varied L1 coefficients; evaluated SAE reconstructions spliced into the model.
rows.baseline: Baseline SAE (1.5× width); no single numeric value stated
rows.value: Gated SAEs offer better reconstruction fidelity at any given L0; no single numeric value stated
rows.note: The paper reports the Pareto-frontier comparison in text; plotted sweep values are not transcribed individually.
rows.check: Gated SAEs recover more loss at every L0 on GELU-1L, but the error does not vanish: the Fig 5 curves stay below 1. That makes this a partial reduction of error by architecture, not full support.

rows.subject: GELU-1L
rows.operation_detail: Measured relative reconstruction bias γ for trained baseline and gated SAEs.

conditions.value: varied L1 coefficient and resulting L0

rows.measure: Relative reconstruction bias γ; γ=1 is unbiased and γ<1 indicates shrinkage
rows.baseline: Baseline SAEs have γ<1, with shrinkage worsening as L1 coefficient increases and L0 decreases
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe gated reconstructions as unbiased and baseline reconstructions as affected by shrinkage.
rows.check: γ measures reconstruction bias, not the size of the error. It is observed only for the shrinkage component (gated γ≈1, baseline γ<1).

source_check.correct: State: partial for V6. Gated γ≈1 and baseline γ<1 establish removal of shrinkage; γ does not measure how much total reconstruction error training artifacts explain.
source_check.problem: Observed describes the shrinkage correction, but overstates the linked V6 claim about predominantly training-related error.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated relative reconstruction bias γ for gated and baseline SAEs.

conditions.value: MLP outputs, attention outputs pre-linear, and residual stream

rows.baseline: Baseline SAEs; individual values not stated in the text summary
rows.value: Gated SAEs resolve shrinkage; individual values not stated in the text summary
rows.note: The text states that the Figure 14 result generalizes the shrinkage finding to Pythia-2.8B.
rows.check: Same caveat as R2. Table values make it readable: Pythia baseline attention γ ranges 0.55–0.93 and gated γ ≈0.99–1.01 (Tables 5, 7).

source_check.correct: Pythia layers: 4, 12, 16, 20, 28, supported by Tables 5–8. Figure 14 names Pythia in its caption but displays layers 6, 13, 20, 27, creating an internal source inconsistency. State: partial for V6; shrinkage correction alone does not establish predominant training attribution.
source_check.problem: The Figure 14 layer reference is inconsistent with the Pythia tables, and the state overgeneralizes from shrinkage to V6.

rows.subject: GELU-1L
rows.operation_detail: Added learned rescale and shift parameters to a frozen baseline SAE while keeping its encoder and decoder directions fixed.

conditions.value: Baseline + rescale & shift vs equal-width baseline and gated SAE

rows.measure: Relative reconstruction bias and loss recovered
rows.baseline: Frozen baseline SAE; no single numeric value stated
rows.value: Rescale and shift resolve shrinkage and improve performance a little, but explain only a small part of the gated SAE performance gain
rows.note: This comparison supports shrinkage as a training-related effect, while indicating it does not account for all the reconstruction-fidelity improvement.
rows.check: Correctly marked partial. Fixing shrinkage alone closes only a small part of the gap, so this specific training artifact explains little of the error.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared gated and baseline SAE training across sites and layers at equal training compute.

conditions.value: MLP outputs, attention outputs pre-linear, and residual stream
Gated vs baseline; Pareto frontier of L0 and loss recovered

rows.baseline: Baseline SAEs; no single numeric value stated
rows.value: Gated SAEs are a Pareto improvement at all tested sites; the maximum loss recovered in every plot was from a gated SAE
rows.note: This is the authors’ aggregate description of the site and layer comparisons.
rows.check: Pareto improvement at all Pythia sites, but large error remains at some sites. For example, gated attention L12 loss recovered is 73–82% and MLP L28 is 73–84% (Tables 7–8). So the error shrinks without disappearing.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1; Appendix B; Figure 12 caption; Tables 7–8.

rows.subject: Gemma-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared gated and baseline SAE training across sites and layers at equal training compute.

conditions.value: MLP outputs, attention outputs pre-linear, and residual stream
Gated vs baseline; Pareto frontier of L0 and loss recovered

rows.baseline: Baseline SAEs; no single numeric value stated
rows.value: Figure 13 compares the Pareto frontiers; the text notes an anomaly at the layer 27 attention-output site, where loss recovered exceeds 1.0 because mean ablation can lower loss on the evaluation data
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 13 and accompanying discussion
rows.note: The paper discusses the layer 27 attention-output anomaly but does not give a single aggregate numerical comparison for all sites.
rows.check: The value field describes an anomaly rather than the result. Appendix B: gated outperforms baseline at all but one MLP/residual site. The layer-27 attention loss recovered >1 is a dataset artefact. Gemma MLP L6 gated reaches only 74–91% loss recovered (Table 3).

relationships.condition: GELU-1L and Pythia-2.8B, Gated vs L1 baseline at equal compute
relationships.reason: Changing the architecture and loss alone lowers the reconstruction error (higher loss recovered) at every L0, so part of the error is a training artifact (R1, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Changing the architecture and loss increased language-model loss recovery at every tested L0 on GELU-1L and Pythia-2.8B.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: GELU-1L and Pythia-2.8B, Gated vs L1 baseline at equal compute
source_check.reason: R1 and R5 demonstrate partial, training-sensitive improvements. Their stated conclusion establishes that some error depends on training, which is weaker than V6. Predominant attribution and exclusion of representation structure remain untested.

relationships.condition: Shrinkage-only fix (rescale & shift), GELU-1L; shrinkage measurements GELU-1L/Pythia
relationships.reason: Gated removes shrinkage (R2, R3), but removing shrinkage alone recovers only a small part of the gain (R4), so shrinkage is a minor contributor to the error.
relationships.display_finding: Gated SAEs removed shrinkage, but rescaling and shifting alone recovered only a small part of their reconstruction improvement.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Shrinkage-only fix (rescale & shift), GELU-1L; shrinkage measurements GELU-1L/Pythia
source_check.reason: R4 shows that eliminating shrinkage explains only a small part of the gated-SAE gain. This qualifies the shrinkage explanation specifically; it does not quantify shrinkage's share of total reconstruction error.

relationships.condition: Gemma-7B sites, and harder Pythia sites (attention L12, MLP L28)
relationships.reason: Even the better architecture leaves substantial loss unrecovered, and Gemma has one site with no gated gain (R5, R6; Tables 3, 7, 8). The error shrinks with architecture but does not mostly disappear.
relationships.display_finding: Substantial language-model loss remained unrecovered at the harder Pythia and Gemma sites, and one Gemma site showed no Gated improvement.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Gemma-7B sites, and harder Pythia sites (attention L12, MLP L28)
source_check.reason: R5 and R6 show incomplete recovery and site dependence, including one Gemma MLP/residual site without an improvement. Pythia gated loss recovered is 73.09–82.04% at attention L12 and 73.3–83.68% at MLP L28. Remaining loss does not itself establish a predominantly non-training cause.

relation.reason: The study intervenes on SAE architecture and training loss and measures reconstruction fidelity and shrinkage.

tranche.reason: Architecture comparisons and the shrinkage ablation bear on a qualified V6: training choices affect reconstruction, while the predominant causal attribution remains untested.

source_check.notes: Loss recovered is normalized downstream cross-entropy recovery, not a fraction of activation MSE or dark-matter variance. The pack truncates several row descriptions; Figure 14 also has a caption/layer inconsistency, although the Pythia tables independently support shrinkage correction.

statements.correction: Section 5.2 isolates shrinkage correction from changes in learned directions. No quantitative partition of total error into training artifacts and representation structure is reported.
statements.problem: The attribution is untested, but this paper does not explicitly formulate or leave open a quantitative dark-matter attribution; that characterization is an inference from its experimental scope.

statements.correction: Figure 9: rescaling and shifting resolve shrinkage but explain only a small part of the gated-SAE performance improvement. Majority attribution of total error is not measured.
statements.problem: R4 establishes a small contribution to the gated-versus-baseline performance gain, not a measured fraction of total error remaining.
